title: When Gut Microbes Run Low on Fiber, They Start Eating Your Intestinal Lining
excerpt: Princeton researchers have discovered that fiber-starved gut bacteria turn to consuming the body's protective mucus layer, while identifying a new class of plant proteins that may reshape nutrition science.
body:
• When dietary fiber runs low, gut bacteria switch to consuming the intestine's protective mucus lining, producing harmful metabolites linked to kidney disease and cancer complications.
  • Princeton researchers identified "Prif" — proteins imitating fiber — a new class of indigestible plant proteins that steer gut microbes toward producing beneficial compounds.
  • The findings, published in PNAS and Nature Metabolism in July 2026, could reshape dietary guidelines and nutritional labeling.
  • Many metabolites previously attributed solely to gut bacteria are also produced by human cells, complicating probiotic therapy strategies.

Starve your gut bacteria of fiber and they may start eating you — literally. New research from Princeton University shows that when plant-based nutrients run low, some intestinal microbes turn on their host and begin consuming the protective mucus lining of the gut, producing toxic byproducts linked to kidney disease and poor cancer outcomes.

The findings, published across two studies in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences and Nature Metabolism in July 2026, also reveal a previously overlooked class of nutrients that could change how scientists think about diet and gut health.

The Fiber-Mucus Connection

Led by Ludwig Princeton researchers Jenna AbuSalim and director Joshua Rabinowitz, the team used isotope-labeled proteins to trace exactly what gut bacteria consume and what they produce.

The results drew a sharp line. Beneficial phenol metabolites — phenylpropionate and hippuric acid, associated with gut health and healthy body weight — were made almost exclusively from indigestible plant proteins in the diet. Harmful phenols — p-cresol sulfate and phenol sulfate, linked to kidney disease toxicity and worse cancer outcomes — came largely from bacteria breaking down the host's own proteins, including those in the mucus lining the intestinal wall.

"The lesson we're learning from studying the interaction of fiber, gut microbes and the intestinal barrier system is that if you don't feed them, they can eat you."

— Joshua Rabinowitz, Director, Ludwig Princeton

That mucus layer is critical. It forms the barrier separating trillions of gut microbes from the intestinal cells beneath them. When bacteria run short of dietary fiber, some species switch to this host-supplied material as an alternative fuel source, thinning the barrier and opening the door to infection and inflammation.

The Discovery of Prif

Beyond confirming fiber's protective role, the research uncovered something unexpected: indigestible plant proteins play a major role in shaping gut health that scientists had largely missed.

Proteins are generally expected to be broken down and absorbed in the upper digestive tract. But the Princeton team found that some plant proteins resist digestion and reach the colon, where gut bacteria process them much like fiber. They named these proteins "Prif" — short for proteins imitating fiber.

"We think Prifs represent an emerging class of dietary nutrients that shape the composition of the gut microbiome and could have a far-reaching influence on metabolic health."

— Jenna AbuSalim, Ludwig Princeton

Fiber suppresses bacterial breakdown of gut mucus, reducing harmful metabolite production. Prif supplies additional dietary protein to microbes farther along the digestive tract, boosting production of beneficial compounds. Together, they shift the balance decisively toward better gut health.

Rabinowitz suggested that food packaging may eventually list Prif right below fiber — a fundamental change to nutritional labeling.

The Body Makes These Compounds Too

The Nature Metabolism study tackled a second assumption: that certain metabolites are exclusively produced by gut bacteria. Using isotope tracing in mice, rats, and human cells, the researchers found that mammalian metabolism independently produces many of the same indole and phenol compounds — including indole-3-lactate and indole-3-acetate.

This matters for therapy design. Probiotics may help when a compound is primarily microbial in origin. But if human cells produce much of the same metabolite, targeting the microbiome alone may have a smaller effect than expected.

What This Means for Your Diet

The practical takeaway reinforces what nutritionists have long advised: eat a diverse, fiber-rich, plant-based diet every day. Part-time fiber intake is not enough — earlier research showed that even alternating high-fiber and fiber-free days left the mucus layer significantly thinner than consistent fiber consumption.

For those looking to optimize gut health, the new research suggests that whole plant foods — which provide both fiber and Prif — are more effective than purified fiber supplements alone. The studies could eventually inform more targeted dietary recommendations for preventing inflammatory bowel disease, metabolic disorders, and certain cancers.
nri_angle: The findings are relevant to Indian dietary traditions, where plant-based meals rich in lentils, vegetables, and whole grains naturally provide both fiber and the newly identified Prif proteins.
